questions.prompt: Let $X\subset\mathbb R^5$ have the subspace topology. Which statements are correct?

options.A: If $X$ is finite, every function $X\to\mathbb R$ is continuous.
options.B: If every function $X\to\mathbb R$ is continuous, then $X$ is finite.
options.C: If $X$ is compact and infinite, then it is uncountable.
options.D: If $X$ is connected with at least two points, then it is uncountable.

hints: Finite Euclidean subspaces are discrete, but infinite discrete subsets also exist.
A convergent sequence together with its limit is a compact countably infinite counterexample. Use a distance map for connectedness.
questions.solution: A is true because finite metric spaces are discrete and all maps from discrete domains are continuous. B is false: $X=\{(n,0,0,0,0):n\in\mathbb N\}$ is infinite and discrete, so every function on it is continuous. C is false: $X=\{0\}\cup\{(1/n,0,0,0,0):n\in\mathbb N\}$ is closed and bounded in $\mathbb R^5$, hence compact, but countably infinite. D is true: select distinct $a,b\in X$. The continuous function $h(x)=\|x-a\|$ has connected image containing 0 and $\|b-a\|>0$, so its image contains a nondegenerate interval and is uncountable. A countable domain cannot have an uncountable image. Correct labels A,D.
questions.theory: The subspace topology on a Euclidean subset is the metric topology induced by Euclidean distance. A discrete subset has every singleton open in its relative topology, allowing arbitrary real-valued functions to be continuous. Discreteness does not require finiteness; integer lattice points are a standard infinite example. Heine–Borel characterizes compact subsets of finite-dimensional Euclidean space as closed and bounded, and a convergent sequence with its limit is a countably infinite compact set. Thus compactness imposes accumulation behavior, not uncountable cardinality. Connectedness is stronger in this respect: a distance function separates the values of two distinct points, and its connected real image contains an interval. Continuous images preserve connectedness and images of countable sets are countable, producing the cardinality conclusion without assuming a path between the points.

similar_questions.prompt: Is $\{1/n:n\ge1\}$ compact in $\mathbb R$?
similar_questions.solution: No. It is bounded but not closed because zero is a limit point omitted from the set. Adding zero makes it compact by Heine–Borel.

similar_questions.prompt: Can a connected subset of $\mathbb R^5$ have exactly countably infinitely many points?
similar_questions.solution: No. A distance map from one of two distinct points has a connected image containing a positive-length real interval, which is uncountable. Therefore any connected non-singleton subset is uncountable.

questions.prompt: Let $\mathbb R$ have Euclidean topology and $\mathbb R_l$ the lower-limit topology with basic intervals $[a,b)$. Which statements are correct?

options.A: Every nonempty connected subspace of $\mathbb R_l$ has one element.
options.B: $\mathbb R_l$ contains a countable dense subset.
options.C: Every open cover of $\mathbb R$ has a countable subcover.
options.D: Every countable open cover of $\mathbb R$ has a finite subcover.

hints: Use a half-line cut to separate any two lower-limit points, and rational density for basic intervals.
For Euclidean $\mathbb R$, use a countable base for Lindelöfness and the increasing cover $(-n,n)$ against countable compactness.
questions.solution: A is true: if a subspace contains $x<y$, the sets $(-\infty,y)$ and $[y,\infty)$ are disjoint open sets in the lower-limit topology, and their intersections give a separation of the subspace. B is true because every nonempty basic $[a,b)$ contains a rational strictly between its endpoints, so $\mathbb Q$ is dense. C refers in the exact source to ordinary $\mathbb R$. Its countable base of rational-endpoint intervals yields a countable subcover: for each basis interval contained in a covering member, select one such member; the selected members cover every point. D is false: the countable open cover $\{(-n,n):n\ge1\}$ covers $\mathbb R$ but no finite subcollection does. Hence A,B,C hold. If C were interpreted for $\mathbb R_l$, the conclusion still holds by the Sorgenfrey line Lindelöf theorem, but that stronger result is not needed for the printed ordinary-$\mathbb R$ claim.
questions.theory: The lower-limit topology, also called the Sorgenfrey topology, refines the usual topology using half-open intervals $[a,b)$ as basic neighborhoods. Half-line cuts are clopen and separate distinct points, so its connected components are singletons. Rational numbers still meet every basic neighborhood, showing separability despite the finer topology. The Euclidean real line is second countable, and every second-countable space is Lindelöf: a countable basis can extract countably many covering members. Lindelöfness asks for countable subcovers of arbitrary open covers; countable compactness asks for finite subcovers of countable covers. They are different properties, and the unbounded increasing interval cover disproves countable compactness of the real line. The Sorgenfrey line is also Lindelöf but not second countable, so separability alone should not be used as a general proof of Lindelöfness.

similar_questions.prompt: Why is $[0,1)$ clopen in the lower-limit line?
similar_questions.solution: It is a basic open set. Its complement $(-\infty,0)\cup[1,\infty)$ is open: each point has a lower-limit basic neighborhood contained in the relevant half-line. Hence the interval is closed as well.

similar_questions.prompt: Does the cover $\{(-n,n):n\ge1\}$ disprove Lindelöfness of ordinary $\mathbb R$?
similar_questions.solution: No. It is already a countable subcover of itself, so it is consistent with Lindelöfness. It disproves compactness and countable compactness because no finite selection covers the unbounded line.
